finding: The `all` row of §2's table reads "no non-`PASS` row in the round carries any severity". Read either way that sentence makes a non-PASS row that carries NO severity harmless under `all`, so a round holding only such rows would be stamped clean. That is not the behaviour tp ships: internal/cli/audit_record.go:71 is `clean := findings == 0`, counted at line 248 through engine.AuditRowIsPass, which is byte-exact on `status` and never reads `severity` at all. So the default the release calls behaviour-preserving (§1 deliverable 1: "the behaviour tp ships today, so a project that does not set it sees no change") changes on install for every project whose auditors omit `severity` — and §7 test 8 puts `null` and absent severities in scope by its own construction. I cannot write task acceptance for the `all` half of the predicate from this text: the sentence and §1 give opposite answers and only the tree breaks the tie.
suggestion: Phrase the `all` row over existence rather than over severity: "no non-`PASS` row exists in the round" — which is `findings == 0` and is exactly what ships. Keep severity out of the `all` row entirely; it is only the `blocking` row that needs to grade. The paragraph below the table already explains why the population is the non-PASS rows, so nothing else needs to change.

finding: "`blocking` governs `clean` and nothing else" is falsified by the two sinks that consume `clean`, and the spec never says which behaviour is wanted. `next_action` is derived FROM `clean` at both audit outputs: internal/cli/audit_record.go:125 calls engine.AuditNextAction(specPath, converged, !clean) and audit_record.go:390 computes latestHasFindings := len(rounds) > 0 && !rounds[len(rounds)-1].Clean. Each site carries a comment asserting the equivalence this release breaks — "the just-recorded round is the latest, so its non-PASS rows are exactly !clean" and "the latest recorded round holding open non-PASS rows is exactly !Clean". Under `blocking`, the first clean round of a streak that still holds `warning`/`info` rows flips next_action from branch 2 ("address the findings, then re-audit") to branch 3 ("run the next audit round") with nothing anywhere naming the rows that were accepted — the same invisibility §4 exists to fix, on the one command §4 says the breakdown is NOT on. I have to invent this behaviour: §2 enumerates three surfaces that stay severity-blind (role_streaks[].open, consecutive_clean, spec_coverage_clean_rounds) and next_action is in neither that list nor the governed one.
suggestion: Add next_action to one of §2's two lists and say which branch a clean-with-open-rows round takes. Either it stays severity-blind (pass the non-PASS count, not !clean, so branch 2 still fires and the operator is still told rows are open), or it follows `clean` (branch 3) and §4's breakdown has to reach --record too, which Non-Goal 4 currently forbids. Also note in §6 that the two invariant comments at audit_record.go:124 and :389 stop being true, so the implementer does not leave them behind as the release's third and fourth false shipped claims.

finding: §4 pins two of by_severity's four input cases and leaves the key type undecidable for the other two. "A row with an unrecognised severity is counted under the literal it carries, and one with none under `null`" — but by_severity is a JSON object, so `null` cannot be a key; it has to be the STRING "null", or the string "", or an omitted bucket, and the three are different payloads for the agent that parses them. Two further cases have no answer at all: a row whose `severity` key is absent (distinct from present-and-null, and §7 test 8 makes that distinction load-bearing for the predicate), and a row whose severity is a non-string JSON value. The twin loop shows what happens by default: audit_merge.go:65 does `status, _ := r["status"].(string)`, so a non-string lands in the empty-string bucket silently. §4's own justification — "the breakdown never hides a row the predicate would block on" — is exactly what these three cases decide, and test 13 ("correct over a mixed round") pins no key name, so an implementation bucketing all three under "" passes it.
suggestion: Name the keys. E.g.: an unrecognised string severity is its own key; a `severity` that is JSON null, absent, or not a string is counted under the single key "unrecognized" (or three named keys, if they should stay distinct). Then have test 13 assert the key names, not just presence — a breakdown whose bucket names are unspecified cannot be read by the agent it is emitted for.

finding: Round 8's record-time decision leaves "the consuming sink" with no referent I can resolve. If `clean` is stamped at record time and nothing recomputes live, then `tp audit --record` is the ONLY command that ever reads the resolved value — `--status`, `--status --check`, `tp resume` and `tp run` all walk stored `clean` flags through engine.ConsecutiveClean/Converged and never touch the field. So §2's "refused at ... the consuming sink (a validation error)" names one command, while "on the same terms and with the same hint as `review_converge_on`" points at a twin that validates the stored value at review --status AND review --record because both consume it. An implementer has to decide whether `tp audit --status` loads and validates a field it does not use — and the two readings differ in an observable way: under one, a project with a typo in .tp/config.json gets exit 1 from --status; under the other it gets exit 0 and a convergence verdict computed from a config it never checked. §7 test 3's "two exit codes, two commands" counts the write command and one consuming command, so it passes either way.
suggestion: Name the consuming commands explicitly — "`tp audit --record` is the only consuming sink; --status, --check and resume read stored verdicts and do not resolve the field" is a legitimate answer and is one sentence. If --status should validate anyway (parity with the twin, so a bad config is caught before a round is spent), say that instead and make test 3 assert the command by name.

finding: The fence as specified has no exemption for a write that changes nothing, and `tp import` is where that bites. §3 fences "every path that writes the field" on the field rather than the direction, and §7 test 11 requires `tp import` to exit 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 "for both `all` and `blocking`". But import does not set a value — it writes a whole task file, workflow block included (engine.LoadTaskWorkflowOverride reads that block and §2 makes the task layer a legal home for the field). So a project that has committed `audit_converge_on` in its <base>.tasks.json can never run `tp import` under `tp run`: the decompose→import unit exits 2 on a file whose value the operator himself committed and which the run would resolve to identically either way. The cap fields avoid this precisely by comparing against the resolved value (engine.UnattendedRaise, and cli/unattended.go's refuseUnattendedRaise), and §3's argument against a direction-scoped fence — "a unit that can set `all` can set `blocking` on the next line" — is an argument about `tp set`, not about a bulk import of an unchanged file.
suggestion: Say what import does with a value that already resolves. Either exempt a write whose resulting resolved value is unchanged (the fence still stops a unit introducing or flipping the field, which is the failure §3 names), or state that a project adopting this field cannot import unattended and must escalate — and then say so where an operator will read it before adopting the field, not only in the fence section.

finding: §2 validates an invalid literal at "the write sink" (singular) while §3 enumerates three write paths, and the two sets are not reconciled. `tp set --workflow` and `tp set --workflow --project` clearly reject a bad literal with a usage error; `tp import`, which §3 explicitly adds to the write paths, has no stated behaviour for a task file whose workflow block carries `audit_converge_on: "blokking"`. Today import writes such a block through the presence-tracked override with no per-value check, so the choice is mine: reject at import (exit 2, matching "the write sink"), or accept it and let it surface later as the consuming sink's exit 1. §7 test 3 pins two commands and cannot discriminate, so whichever I pick ships ungraded.
suggestion: Add `tp import` to the sentence that names the write sink, with its exit code — or state that import is fenced but not validating, and that an invalid literal arriving through import is caught at the consuming sink. One clause either way.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught and NOT a defect. I was about to report that §6's second reversal ("the docs-contract guard pinning a `SKILL.md` sentence") names one document while internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go asserts the same substring for README.md too — which would make the reversal incomplete and the guard still red after the specified edit. Checked before writing it: the guard asserts divergenceCountingSubstring against skills/tp/SKILL.md only (docs_contract_test.go:131-133), and its own header records that v0.34.0 §8.1 moved the driver-facing summary out of README.md. A literal search confirms README.md does not carry the sentence. §6 is exactly right; the finding would have been false.
suggestion: No change. Recorded so the same near-miss is not re-derived by a later round.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught and NOT a defect. §2's "resolved *task override > project config > built-in* — the precedence workflow fields actually use; there is no CLI layer and no `TP_<FIELD>` layer for one" contradicts CLAUDE.md's parenthetical "(CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in)", and I nearly reported the spec as wrong. engine.ResolveWorkflowLayers takes exactly two override layers plus a built-in default block and reads no environment: the spec is correct and CLAUDE.md's parenthetical is the stale one. Reported here rather than as a spec finding because it is a repository-doc defect outside this spec's surface.
suggestion: No spec change. If anyone is fixing CLAUDE.md's Project Configuration line later, that parenthetical is the one to re-derive.
